utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, you were. This is case number IT-03-69-PT, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the parties make their appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, good afternoon, Your Honour, David Re assisted by our case manager Ms. Skye Winner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For Mr. Stanisic, myself, Wayne Jordash, and Melinda Taylor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is Mr. Knoops not coming today?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm Zoran Jovanovic appearing on behalf of Mr. Franko Simatovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. This is the sixth Status Conference with the previous one being the one that took place on 20th of January this year, and this Status Conference was due originally last month, but upon the request of the parties I postponed it to today. Although we passed the 112 days provided by the Rules, I don't see any problem there given that there were consent of all the parties involved and that the accused are on provisional release. First of all, I deal with the matters. There's one thing I'd like to raise with the parties, in particular the Mr. Stanisic Defence. I was handed over a memorandum from Mr. Knoops by the senior legal officer of our Chamber, a memorandum addressed to me titled "Defence memorandum on preparation for the Status Conference on the 3rd of June, 2005," which is partly to be confidential. I note that it is of great assistance for the Chamber, for the Pre-Trial Judge, to deal with the matter, because it can serve as a summary of the submission of the party, but given that it contains a substantial and detailed submission of the party, I would prefer such document to be filed officially. Could that be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that there are several motions outstanding at this moment. Two most important of them being -- one of them is motion for the amendment of indictment from the Prosecution, and we, the Chamber, granted the motion from the Defence from the extension of time for response until the motion till the access to ex parte materials be resolved. That decision will be filed, delivered in due course very shortly, sometime hopefully in the next week. And then we have a bigger motion, motion for joinder from the Prosecution. I wonder if that motion has any effect on the motion for the amendment of indictment at all. If Mr. Re can give some explanation on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the moment they stand separately. The motion to amend the indictment is only in respect of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic. No similar motion has been proposed in the Seselj, Hadzic, or Martic case. The Prosecution's position is the Trial Chamber should proceed to deal with that matter separately because the motions which have been filed in relation to Martic, Seselj, and Simatovic and Stanisic I think were going to the bureau and the two are essentially separate matters. If the Trial Chamber or the bureau decides to join the indictments of the various accused any indictment coming out of that which would have to be a joint indictment would deal with that separate issue of the amendment and whether it applies to one or all of the accused on an amended joined indictment. Does that assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure whether it is for the bureau to decide upon the issue. But can I take it that the Prosecution's position is that once decided to join them we'll have one joint indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That would be the case. When I say the bureau, I understand the process was the bureau was getting the Trial Chambers together to decide on it as opposed to making the decision itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any observation from the Defence on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The only observation I would make is that the timing of the response to joinder, I would respectfully submit, ought to be extended to allow the decision on the amendment in relation to Stanisic and Simatovic indictment to be decided first. We ought to then be allowed to look at what the indictment is after that decision before having to consider the joinder decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the motion when it is filed from the Defence for the extension of time for response.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to deal with the -- some disclosure issue. I understand that there are some dispute or disagreement between the parties upon some certain translation issues. Can I hear from the Defence, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it relates specifically Witness B024, but it may well relate to others, but the Defence wrote to the Prosecution request service of a B/C/S transcript of B024's interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is taped into video, so you mean the transcription of that video?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Transcription of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand English transcript has been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's right. And what we're seeking is the Prosecution to disclose the B/C/S transcript version so that the accused can study that interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding is that the actual video hasn't been disclosed because of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- certain protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's right. The Prosecution take the view that by disclosing the video the accused would recognise the voice and that would breach the protective measures order. We don't seek to go behind that. What we seek to have instead, therefore, is disclosure of the B/C/S transcript. The Prosecution's response in a letter dated the 1th of April, 2005 is simply to say we do not have the B/C/S transcript of the interview; the witness subject of protective measures; the Prosecution do not provide a copy of the audiotape as his voice would be known by the accused. Full stop. They don't go on to deal with their position in relation to whether they consider they've complied with their disclosure obligations simply by taking that position. We would say in order to properly comply with their disclosure obligations they ought to serve a B/C/S transcript to allow the accused to be able to know the case against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the issue will be whether Prosecution has obligation to translate those transcription into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Exactly. In the absence of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the absence of the Serb version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And serving the video, which they do not which to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I hear the Prosecution's position. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution's position is that we have complied with our disclosure obligations. We have provided the Defence with a copy of the transcript in English in a very timely fashion. They -- we do not have a B/C/S transcript. It hasn't been done. Nothing, of course, prevents the Defence from translating it themselves or requesting a translation from CLSS or do an informal one themselves if they wish it to be done. It's not an issue of the Prosecution feeling -- not providing the audio because it feels that the voice would identify the person being interviewed, there's a Trial Chamber order for delayed disclosure of 30 days before trial. Our position is that we've complied and there's nothing more we wish to say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Prosecution's case is that this is different from the obligation of disclosing witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where the Prosecution has obligation to translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Into the language the accused understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I will also note there's a similar problem in -- I wonder whether I can name these suspects [sic]. Can I go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Different from a protected witness, Mr. Babic's case is a bit different I would assume. There's a similar problem in relation to Babic suspect interviews, and the Prosecution takes the same position, but my query is whether Prosecution has any translation of the transcription in -- given -- considering the Rule 43(vi), because let me find the -- read the: "Whenever the Prosecutor questions a suspect, the questioning shall be audio-recorded or video-recorded, in accordance with the following procedure," and then subparagraph (vi) says "the tape shall be transcribed if the suspect becomes an accused." I have to note that Mr. Babic has already become an accused so I assume the Prosecution should already have the transcription -- sorry, the translation into B/C/S of that transcription.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. There's definitely the English one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought the issue was the plea agreement not the suspect interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is the suspect interviews. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's different from 68 material. The suspect interview is also in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is the I view that we would wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Our view of the Rule is the same as I outlined earlier: The transcription is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should be in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- in English or French, the official languages of the Tribunal. We have provided it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having noted the Prosecution position and if the Defence still wants the translation of those English transcription, it should file the motion and the Chamber will consider the issue. Any further observation, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would only make this observation: We would say the Rule is quite clear Rule 66 on this issue. And whilst we accept Your Honour's direction to file a motion, we are almost overwhelmed in this case by the mass of material. And filing motions on issues such as this places an even greater burden on us where we would say the Prosecution obligation is crystal clear. Those are my observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could cite the jurisprudence which exists already. Speaking for myself, I think it is not crystal clear whether 66(A)(ii) covers the transcription of suspect interview, videotaped interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would simply say plain reading of the rules -- I don't have the jurisprudence at my finger tips --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would appreciate --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the Defence would file a motion on this issue. Then we have an issue in relation to 68 materials. Yes. I understand the Defence is seeking the plea agreement of certain accused. Can I hear from the Defence first on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The -- what we're seeking is the statements underlying the plea agreement and would simply say that they fall, we would submit, under Rule 68 obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To which the Prosecution do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: They do not agree. There has been correspondence, and I think that this particular witness we're referring to is subject to protective measures, but it has been dealt with in correspondence in April and May and the Prosecution do not accept that they have an obligation to disclose that agreement or the underlying statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not for the Prosecution to determine whether a certain material is exculpatory or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it is for the Prosecution to determine that. We accept that. After a review of the material, we take note that -- but we are concerned because we have, for example, disclosed a pre-trial brief and the Prosecution have not, it appears, reviewed that in order to fulfil their Rule 68 obligations, and we're concerned in relation to this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. specific witness that the same might be true. We accept, of course, that it's within their jurisdiction, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said after a review of the material. Do you mean you reviewed that very material?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, after -- the Prosecution's obligation extends to reviewing the material and then making a decision as to Rule 68 material. We would say that there are concerns that they haven't done it in relation to the pre-trial brief and they may not have done it in relation to this identified witness. That's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Re, the refusal, if I can say so, from the Prosecution to disclose those materials is based on the fact that -- or assessment of the Prosecution that they are not exculpatory. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. There are two issues which my learned friend Mr. Jordash raised. The first one is the two plea agreements. The two plea agreements were filed confidentially in the two cases concerned. One of them is as about irrelevant to this particular indictment as you could possibly get. The other one contains nothing exculpatory or in any way affecting the credibility of the proposed witness which isn't referred to in the judgement. Sorry, there's nothing in that plea agreement which isn't in the judgement anyway. The fact is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exculpatory, being different from about relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They're not relevant. They're not exculpatory. They don't affect the credibility. They're filed confidentially and we've made it clear if the Defence wishes to gain access to these they simply file a motion before Trial Chamber I for access to it. I doubt we'll oppose the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt here. The confidentiality itself cannot be an obstacle for the -- to the disclosure of 68 materials. Once Prosecutor finds that material exculpatory it has the duty to get the permission from the Chamber to disclose those materials to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, of course. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the issue is not confidentiality but exculpatoriness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are two subissues there. One is there is nothing Rule 68. We have reviewed it. As Your Honour has correctly pointed out the law, we have reviewed it. There's nothing there which in our view could possibly be Rule 68 which moves to the fact that the Defence wants to get hold of these. If they wish to do so they must file a motion before the relevant Trial Chamber and we've told them that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether Prosecution cannot take it as the Defence is invoking 66(B) disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I suppose that if you took it at its most technical in relation to one of them, possibly. Possibly. In relation to the other one, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I can understand the other one. If the Defence can elaborate on the relevant of that, the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution doesn't mind if they mention the names publicly. We don't think there's any -- any need for confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be Mr. Jokic, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic. We say it's irrelevant because it concerns the shelling of Dubrovnik in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That particular witness, as from the pre-trial brief, that person had a relationship with Bogdanovic who was in the Ministry of the Interior. Clearly related closely in time and activities to the accused. We are not simply asking for the plea agreement. The letter we sent to the Prosecution asked for the plea bargain, the factual basis for the plea bargain or witness statements from Admiral Jokic which relate to the role of the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Interior in Croatia. That's the relevance, we would say, and we would say that would upon a proper review give rise to a decision that that material in part at least is exculpatory. That is clear, we would submit, from the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, having heard from the Prosecution that they find those materials not exculpatory to the Defence, the reasonable steps for the Defence to take is to go to the Chamber and get the permission for access to those materials, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I simply just leave at it at this, then, Your Honour, that when the Prosecution wrote back to the Defence, notwithstanding the request for a number of items revolving around the plea agreement, the Prosecution's response dealt only with the plea agreement. It might assist the Defence in terms of knowing whether to submit a motion or not to know whether the Prosecution have in fact reviewed all that material or in fact have simply reviewed the plea agreement as indicated by their letter. If it's the former, that they reviewed all that material, it may mean that a motion is pointless. But if they have limited themselves to the plea agreement, they might in the spirit of cooperation want to look at the other material first before we then are obliged to take a decision as to whether to draft a motion. I don't know if the Prosecution want to assist in indicating the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, we have reviewed the material related to Admiral Jokic and as far as I know there's nothing there which could be Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There was one other issue which Mr. Jordash commented or arose in relation to Rule 68, and that was -- I think he said that we had, he suspected, failed to comply with our obligation because we hadn't read the pre-trial brief and done searches looking for exculpatory material. In as much as that may be a live issue here and was raised at the Rule 65 ter conference the other day and in correspondence between the parties, we have made our view clear to the Defence that we invite them to provide us with relevant search terms which they consider relevant to their defence, and we will run the requisite searches through the material they would not have access to on the Electronic Disclosure Suite, namely witness material and Rule 70 material. We make it quite clear from reading, as the Defence suggests, the index to the pre-trial brief it tells us virtually nothing. It's an index of subject headings. We are not a position to second-guess the Defence tactics or the exact nature of what they're after or what could be exculpatory. We are basing it upon our own assessments. If they wish us to assist them in the most practical manner, we invite them to provide us with search terms and we can run the searches.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just briefly reply. It's not -- it was a concern I expressed. I'm not making any firm allegations, but what we do say is that we will provide more in the -- by way of search terms although we do say that the pre-trial brief is fairly detailed. But we hear what the Prosecution say and search terms will be forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Since the Prosecution's position is clarified, I leave the matter to the Defence. What happened to the statements of Mr. Bogdanovic and Janackovic? Have they been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was actually reviewing them today, so that -- I'll be in a position to communicate with the Defence sometime next week on whether they should be disclosed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And has the video in issue been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The video in issue is sitting on the floor next to me and we will hand it to the Defence immediately after the conclusion of this Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On that subject, I'm sorry to leap to my feet, but I would like to express a further concern about that video. It was, as Your Honour knows, subject to special measures. We haven't received it, notwithstanding an order of May the 11th that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know that until I entered the courtroom today, and actually theoretically speaking or practically speaking, the Prosecution should be in breach of that protective measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But now I think that kind of protective measure is of no use at this moment. I'll discuss the mat we are the Chamber and try to lift that confidentiality very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, that's my concern, simply put: special measures. We haven't been allowed to see the video. The rest of the world has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think there are some three or four matters Mr. Stanisic's Defence would like to raise, but considering that I have read those submission handed over to me by way of Senior Legal Officer, I wonder there is anything for the Chamber, Trial Chamber, to practically do anything at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was simply to bring the information to Your Honour's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And the Chamber will take note of it, and again if there is any specific relief the Defence is seeking, I would encourage the Defence to file a motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having dealt with these matters, I wonder if there's anything further for the parties to raise. Yes, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There's an issue I'd like to raise, and this is something that was discussed at the 65 ter meeting, so I believe you're familiar with the substance of this issue. It's about the application of Rule 92 bis. At the previous status conference, the OTP provided an explanation to the effect that the Prosecution's motion on adopting witness statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis is part of the 65 ter motion or, rather, that the summaries contained in the motion itself were printed in two different ways. Everything that was printed in italics is what the Prosecution wishes to submit according to Rule 92 bis. Now the problem emerges in relation to those witnesses where a partial 92 bis admission has been proposed. The Defence does not believe that there are sufficient elements for us to agree with the proposal of the other party regarding the use of this Rule. The Defence has initiated two further meetings in the meantime with the other party in a bid to resolve this problem. However, the situation remains the same for both parties. Why is it that I say that the Defence can't declare a final position on the application of Rule 92 bis at this time? There have been several examples demonstrating a degree of imprecision. We have the same summaries in both sections, and it's not clear which summaries Rule 92 bis would apply to and which not. In relation to one specific witness, there has been a motion to admit his statement pursuant to Rule 92 bis, but there is no portion of the text in italics in that particular statement. Therefore, it is impossible for the Defence to ascertain with any degree of certainty which specific portions of these statements are being submitted for admission under Rule 92 bis. I think the problem has been resolved in relation to those witness statements that will be admitted in their entirety under Rule 92 bis. Most of these are crime base witnesses. This can be dealt with swiftly. I do however believe it is necessary for the OTP in relation to those witness statements where only parts of statements are tendered under Rule 92 bis to submit a motion containing all the relevant elements or portions of statements and transcripts that the OTP believes should be tendered under Rule 92 bis. Only then could the Defence state its final position on this matter. In their motion pursuant to Rule 65 ter, the OTP announced that prior to trial they would be providing all relevant details but only once the Defence has marked out the witnesses in relation to which it would accept a 92 bis submission. We believe this is unduly delayed and that this motion containing all the relevant elements should be filed in good time, and then the Defence would be given a chance to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow the last. The Prosecution announced that prior to try they would be providing all relevant details but only once the Defence has marked out the witnesses in relation to which you would accept the 92 bis submission. What does it mean? Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't know. If Mr. Jovanovic could perhaps elaborate I might know what he's meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In actual fact, the OTP interprets most of the 65 ter summaries in the light of their motion asking the Defence to declare our position as regards the statements, the 92 bis statements, we actually accept. It is only once the Defence has made our position known that the OTP would be forwarding more detailed information on the matter. As stated in the 65 ter motion, on page 6, these would be delivered in relation to each and every witness prior to the beginning of the trial, and here I mean the information requested by the Defence. This would make it possible for us to make our position known. I believe it is necessary for the motion to contain references to specific statements or portions of statements in relation to which the OTP has requested 92 bis. I believe this could create a certain amount of confusion as to which portions of these statements would come under Rule 92 bis. Certain statements are repeated in these summaries pursuant to Rule 92 bis. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, but the motion -- was the motion filed or is it in the process of discussion among the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no motion. We clearly can't file a motion until we have a Trial Chamber appointed, because the Trial Chamber will decide the issue, not the Pre-Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has been our practice that -- to defer those matters to the actual Trial Chamber. But the discussion can take place during the pre-trial process, which no doubt would be of assistance to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Trial Chamber if the parties come to an agreement as to admission of 92 bis, full bis or partly bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is our earnest desire that we can do that, and we certainly have about very much exhorted to do so by the senior legal officer, Ms. Featherstone, at every meeting. Of the 120 witnesses on the list, 11 have indicated we would call viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Forty-nine we have indicated are 92 bis, in our view in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: ICTY jargon, full bis. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Fifty-five are partial 92 bis and we have 5 expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Partial bis means that they would come for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And partial examination-in-chief will be dealt with in viva voce as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's correct, although it's the Trial Chamber's decision whether or not those we indicate would be fully 92 bis would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Be it 92 bis or 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Or without cross-examination, but our proposal would be our proposal but we would tender their evidence in chief via statement 92 bis or 89(F). So of the 49 there is absolutely no issue as to which parts of the evidence we say are 92 bis. It's the entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What those statements disclosed --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Everything has been disclosed. Of the 55 in our 65 ter summary filing we have written -- Mr. Groome has indicated this to the Trial Chamber -- to Your Honour before. We have italicised the portions of the summary which we say should be 92 bis and the portions which are not are not italicised or the other way around. Whichever way it is, it's quite clear that we say this portion goes to the actual conducts of the accused and the other part doesn't. Now, our desire is for the Defence to inform us, based on our summaries, whether or not they agree with our assessment, and from there we may be able to reach agreement with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ray. Mr. Jovanovic, I didn't follow when you said you need more detailed information to make any response to this. Once the witness statements are disclosed, what do you need more than that to say you are agreeing with this or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's where the Defence sees the problem. The Prosecution says that they exactly marked the sections of individual statements that are suggested for admission under 92 bis. However, on the basis of the summaries that are printed in two different ways, we simply had a difficulty to identify the parts of witness statements that are intended for 92 bis and those that are not. The Defence has to see how the OTP interprets this and then we're supposed to recognise what section is proposed in which way. This creates difficulties, and that's why I gave examples. We have almost identical statements or, rather, portions of statements within a single text and the Defence cannot discern which part is which. That is why I think - and as I said, again, I'm just talking about partial 92 bis application - the Defence believes that it is the duty of the Prosecution to mark the exact portions of the transcript or statements that they have in mind so that the Defence would not do it on its own on the basis of their own interpretation. They want to have the Prosecution's interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, my understanding is that those parts the Prosecution wishes to introduce by way of 92 bis are italicised, but the -- I see that there's some technical problems I would say. So I would encourage the parties to sit together after this conference to find the solution, sort out the way to go on. So could that be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. We accept this recommendation. However, as I've already said, we have already had two meetings about the same issue. The result is that I'm presenting the problem here and now, yet I do hope that we will make some headway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the discussion must take place in more detailed way. You should bring specific witness statements and bring the attention to the Prosecution to specific parts you have questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what we will do, Your Honour. In the time ahead of us, we will try to deal with the matter through direct meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I take this opportunity to deal with another matter, i.e., the agreed facts. I understand there's not much progress on this, but my understanding is that Prosecution is minded to file in one way or another in a motion or the questions to be put to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We have prepared a draft proposal. After the 65 ter conference a few days ago I spoke with Mr. Knoops and Mr. Jovanovic. We agreed we would send it to them first so we could attempt to reach an agreement to file a joint motion rather than us coming to the Trial Chamber. We should be able to do that in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can it be done very shortly?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Fairly near future, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So can I set a deadline for this? Two weeks from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's to file a joint motion or to reach agreement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, just put the question, questions to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And how long would the Defence need to respond to those questions? I would encourage not too ambitious nor that simple, but try to get as many as -- agreements as possible. Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In response to Your Honour's question, I'm not sure. Until I see what the Prosecution will deliver, it's difficult, and I'm reluctant to commit ourselves, especially in light of the outstanding motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I see the point. You have to communicate with your clients and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in the sense for the purpose of promoting the process, I would set four weeks. Is that too short? And if necessary, you can ask for a leave to extension of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly. If I can allay the Court's fears slightly in relation to the subject we were talking about, the 92 bis, we have spoken to the Prosecution and agreed that we will indicate, as far as we're able from the Rule 65 ter document, which witnesses we say are possibly in principle that we can look at pursuant to that Rule. We will do the same thing with the document if relation to the adjudicated facts and indicate as far as we can our agreement or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So wrapping up, the question for the purpose of the agreements of the facts among the parties should be sent by the end of the 17th of this month. That is the recess time. And the response to that questions should be filed by the end of July, I would say. And file a motion for extension of time if necessary. Is there any matter to raise for the parties? Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There was one matter which Ms. Featherstone raised at the conference the other day and that related to confidential filings, and I think she described it as a tendency or a practice developed to file matters confidentially, not necessarily on the part of the Prosecution. The Prosecution has some concerns about a number of the filings that have been -- the Defence has filed confidentially. There was a recent one which related to a legal issue concerning ex parte materials and a decision the Trial Chamber should make. Our position is that those types of filings should be filed publicly and the only things that should be filed confidentially are matters which are concerned with the safety and protection of victims or witnesses and medical issues related to the accused, the normal sorts of things. And we'd certainly invite the Pre-Trial Chamber to -- if you feel it necessary, to issue some directions. And -- our position is that those sorts of matters should be put in confidential annexes and unless it's absolutely necessary all matters should be conducted publicly before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Defence must have heard it, and I believe they will attend to it. Is there any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just one matter, although if I may just briefly comment on my learned friend's last comments. We hear what the Court has said, and of course we will do our best in that regard. But our filings have been filed in that way as at -- out of an abundance of caution for the protective measures of the witnesses; nothing more, nothing less. So if we've overly interpreted those measures then we apologise but we thought better to err on the side of caution. Secondly, the final issue we'd like to raise is the issue of the confidential testimony and exhibits from the Milosevic trial, simply to raise our concern that the information which remains to be disclosed by the Prosecution may well be the most crucial evidence against Mr. Stanisic, and it's clear from reading some of the witness statements that when issues which might relate to Mr. Stanisic are under discussion, those are the times that the session becomes a closed one, and so we are concerned that we haven't had that information disclosed. We are concerned that the Prosecution's stance thus far had been that they will provide the material, and I quote, "as it becomes available," and I simply raise this issue now to say that we would like the information as soon as possible because our preparation depends upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the status of that issue so far? Was there a motion to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There was a motion, and there is an order that the material is to be served. The Prosecution have accepted their obligations in that regard, and they have indicated that they are endeavouring to do so. They haven't indicated a time frame. Simply I'm flagging the issue up as one of concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I thought I indicated at the pre- -- sorry, the 65 ter conference the other day that an investigator is in the process of contacting all the witnesses who gave evidence in Milosevic and it's a process that we estimated of one to two months to speak to the people and either obtain their consent or give up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would very much encourage the Prosecution to expedite the process and comply with their obligations. No other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is one matter which possibly requires an explanation from the Prosecution. That's in relation to the disclosure of the video. The Prosecution -- the position I think that was taken was we wanted to personally serve it on -- because of the protective measures we wanted to personally serve it on Defence counsel and we understood they were coming for a 65 ter conference and we were intending to serve it then. But the conference was put over for a week and we didn't understand that both were going to be here on Tuesday. That's why we didn't hand it over on Tuesday. We apologise if we appear to be in breach of the Trial Chamber's order. Is certainty wasn't intentional. But because of the issues at the time we wanted personal service but those issues have now disintegrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So to be safe -- on the safe side, there's no position to lift the protective measures from that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly not. Not now, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. My understanding is that next Status Conference should be around the end of September this year, but given the motion for joinder it remains to be seen, and the Scheduling Order will be filed in due course. This hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: at 4.01 p.m.
